newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds flat in lacklustre trade.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds flat in lacklustre trade.

text.p: Irish bonds were broadly unchanged in quiet trade on Friday in the absence of key data and in the midst of a generally slack period for Irish bonds, dealers said.

"Currency concerns and high money market rates have been keeping non-residents at bay recently, and domestic investors don't seem particularly interested either," a dealer said. "We're just not seeing liquidity -- everyone seems to be holding off for the next big event."
By 1450 GMT, the 6.5 percent bond due 2001 was up 10 pence at 102.20 to yield 5.89 percent, while the eight percent bond due 2006 was up 10 pence at 110.08 to yield 6.50 percent.
Yields against German Bunds were broadly unchanged from Thursday's close at 161 basis points over in the five-year bond, and 95 over in the 10-year.
Irish financial markets were largely unmoved on Friday by the widely expected appointment of the fiscally conservative Charlie McCreevy as new finance minister on Thursday.

McCreevy's plans for tax and spending are well known and he is not expected to introduce any changes to the broad EMU-oriented stance of Irish economic policy but the key issue for most market players will be his attitude to the currency which has been buffeted by selling pressure in recent weeks.
Views among economists are mixed on whether the new government will adjust the punt's exchange rate in the ERM to discourage recent speculative selling of the Irish unit.
The selling has been fuelled by the view that currencies will enter the euro at their ERM central parity and the Irish pound is currently trading well above that level.
The weak Irish pound has been causing Irish bonds to underperform against Spain and Italy over recent weeks, dealers said.
Looking ahead, dealers said, international focus next week would be on U.S. payrolls on Friday, an important indicator of Q2 growth.

At home EBR figures on Wednesday and credit data on Thursday would be of interest, particularly EBR which is likely to show a large budget surplus at mid-year and emphasise that there will be limited issuance of fresh stock over the balance of the year.
The value of Irish retail sales fell a provisional seasonally-adjusted 1.5 percent in April, giving a year-on-year increase of 4.9 percent, Central Statistics Office (CSO) data showed on Friday.

In March, the value of retail sales rose 2.4 percent over the month and was up 6.9 percent year-on-year. This was revised from provisional estimates of a 2.5 percent monthly rise and a 7.0 percent rise on the year.
